regional.syndrome: Sudden high fever with severe, often symmetrical polyarthralgia and rash; the name means 'that which bends up'. Arthritis persists for months to years in 30–40%. Neonatal infection from intrapartum transmission and neurological disease in older adults can be severe; deaths occur mainly via decompensation of comorbidity.
regional.headline: Alphavirus of the Semliki Forest complex causing explosive epidemics of febrile polyarthritis.
regional.prevention: Vector control; the virus-like particle vaccine Vimkunya is licensed from 12 years of age. The live-attenuated IXCHIQ was licensed first, but its US licence was suspended in August 2025 and the application withdrawn in January 2026 after vaccine-strain encephalitis and other serious adverse events.
regional.geography: Africa, Asia, Indian Ocean, Americas since 2013, with autochthonous outbreaks in southern Europe.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.incubation: Decades. Myelopathy appears after years; leukaemia typically forty to sixty years after perinatal infection.
regional.syndrome: Lifelong asymptomatic carriage in over 90%. Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL) appears after a latency of forty to sixty years, usually in those infected through breastfeeding, with a lifetime risk of a few per cent; HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP) in under 4%, presenting as spastic paraparesis with bladder dysfunction. Also infective dermatitis of childhood, uveitis, and Strongyloides hyperinfection, the last because the virus distorts the Th2 response that normally contains the worm.
regional.headline: The first human retrovirus discovered, infecting 5-10 million people. Most carry it for life without consequence; a minority develop adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma after decades, or a progressive myelopathy.
regional.prevention: Avoiding breastfeeding by carrier mothers where safe alternatives exist, which is what cut transmission in Nagasaki; leucodepletion and donor screening of blood; condoms; not sharing injecting equipment. No vaccine.
regional.geography: Sharply defined endemic foci rather than a global distribution: south-western Japan, the Caribbean, parts of South America, West and Central Africa, Iran, Romania, and Aboriginal communities of central Australia, where some adult seroprevalences exceed 40%.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.incubation: Years, and progression to AIDS may not occur at all.
regional.syndrome: The same spectrum as HIV-1 — CD4 decline, opportunistic infection, AIDS — but with a longer asymptomatic phase and a substantial minority who never progress. Plasma viral loads are lower at any given CD4 count.
regional.headline: A West African lentivirus from sooty mangabeys, less transmissible and slower to progress than HIV-1, and intrinsically resistant to two whole antiretroviral classes.
regional.prevention: As for HIV-1: pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis, condoms, harm reduction, and prevention of vertical transmission. Tenofovir-based PrEP is active.
regional.geography: West Africa, with the highest prevalences in Guinea-Bissau and Senegal, and cases in Portugal, France and India reflecting historic ties.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Insidious fever, sore throat, retrosternal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea; severe cases develop facial oedema, mucosal bleeding, shock and encephalopathy. Overall community case fatality ~1%, but 15–20% in hospitalised patients. Sensorineural deafness in up to a third of survivors is the hallmark sequela, and third-trimester infection carries very high fetal and maternal mortality.
regional.headline: Rodent-borne arenavirus causing 100,000–300,000 infections and thousands of deaths annually in West Africa.
regional.prevention: Rodent control, safe food storage, hospital infection control; vaccines are in clinical development (CEPI priority).
regional.geography: Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea, Benin, Ghana, Mali, Togo.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Bunyamwera and Germiston viruses: self-limiting fever with headache, rash and arthralgia. Ngari virus: documented haemorrhagic fever outbreaks in Kenya and Somalia, originally mistaken for Rift Valley fever.
regional.headline: Prototype orthobunyavirus. Its reassortant member Ngari virus (Bunyamwera backbone with Batai M segment) causes haemorrhagic fever in East Africa.
regional.geography: Sub-Saharan Africa; Xingu virus in South America.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Fever, headache, backache, rash and occasional mild meningism; self-limiting.
regional.headline: Highly prevalent African orthobunyavirus causing undifferentiated fever; seroprevalence exceeds 50% in parts of East Africa.
regional.geography: Sub-Saharan Africa.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Fever with rash; isolated reports of meningoencephalitis and haemorrhagic manifestations.
regional.headline: Bunyamwera-serogroup virus isolated from African febrile patients, with rare reports of haemorrhagic and neurological presentations.
regional.geography: West, Central and East Africa, Madagascar.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Abrupt fever, profound weakness, myalgia, then vomiting and high-volume diarrhoea with electrolyte derangement, shock and sometimes haemorrhage. Survivors experience uveitis, arthralgia and neurological sequelae; virus persists in semen, aqueous humour and CSF, enabling late sexual transmission and relapse.
regional.headline: Filovirus causing Ebola disease, with case fatality historically 25–90%; now treatable with monoclonal antibodies and preventable by vaccination.
regional.prevention: The rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (Ervebo) used in ring vaccination, plus the Ad26/MVA regimen; safe burial practices and infection prevention and control.
regional.geography: Central and West Africa — the 2013–2016 West African epidemic caused over 28,000 cases.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Dengue fever: high fever, severe headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia/arthralgia ('breakbone fever'), rash. A minority progress at defervescence to dengue with warning signs or severe dengue — plasma leakage, shock, haemorrhage and organ impairment. Secondary infection with a different serotype raises severe-disease risk through antibody-dependent enhancement.
regional.headline: The most important arboviral infection of humans worldwide, with an estimated 100–400 million infections annually.
regional.prevention: Vector control, Wolbachia-based mosquito replacement, and the live-attenuated vaccines CYD-TDV (serostatus-restricted) and TAK-003.
regional.geography: Tropics and subtropics worldwide; expanding with vector range.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Biphasic: an initial fever with headache and myalgia, brief remission, then in ~15% a toxic phase with jaundice, haemorrhage, renal failure and shock; case fatality in the toxic phase is 30–60%.
regional.headline: The prototype flavivirus and the reason the genus is named 'flavi' — a vaccine-preventable viral haemorrhagic fever.
regional.prevention: A single dose of the 17D live-attenuated vaccine gives lifelong protection — one of the most effective vaccines ever made; mandated under International Health Regulations for travel to endemic areas.
regional.geography: Tropical South America and sub-Saharan Africa.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: About 80% of infections are asymptomatic; 20% develop West Nile fever; <1% develop neuroinvasive disease — meningitis, encephalitis or a poliomyelitis-like acute flaccid paralysis, with substantial mortality and long-term sequelae in older adults.
regional.headline: Globally the most widespread encephalitic flavivirus, maintained in a bird–mosquito cycle.
regional.prevention: Mosquito control and personal protection; blood-supply nucleic-acid screening; equine vaccines exist but no human vaccine.
regional.geography: Africa, Europe, Middle East, Asia, Australia (Kunjin), and across the Americas since 1999.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Usually mild or asymptomatic: low-grade fever, maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, arthralgia. Congenital Zika syndrome — microcephaly, cerebral calcification, ocular and joint anomalies — follows infection in pregnancy. Guillain–Barré syndrome is an established post-infectious complication.
regional.headline: Flavivirus whose 2015–2016 American epidemic established it as a human teratogen.
regional.prevention: Vector control, barrier contraception or abstinence after exposure, travel advice in pregnancy. No licensed vaccine.
regional.geography: Africa, Asia, Pacific, Americas.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.incubation: 1–9 days after tick bite; 5–13 days after blood contact.
regional.syndrome: Abrupt fever, myalgia, severe headache, then haemorrhagic manifestations, hepatic dysfunction and DIC. Case fatality ranges from 5% to 40%. Nosocomial outbreaks among healthcare workers are a defining feature.
regional.headline: The most geographically widespread tick-borne virus causing human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen requiring high-level containment.
regional.prevention: Tick protection, safe slaughter practice, and strict barrier nursing with full PPE. No licensed vaccine (a Bulgarian inactivated vaccine has limited use).
regional.geography: Africa, the Balkans, Middle East, Central and South Asia, western China; expanding with Hyalomma range into Spain and southern Europe.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.headline: Mokola virus. Rabies-like fatal encephalitis; human cases reported in Nigeria and Zimbabwe. Critically, it is not neutralised by rabies vaccine-induced antibody, so standard post-exposure prophylaxis cannot be relied on.
regional.geography: Mokola virus. Rabies-like fatal encephalitis; human cases reported in Nigeria and Zimbabwe. Critically, it is not neutralised by rabies vaccine-induced antibody, so standard post-exposure prophylaxis cannot be relied on.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: In animals: encephalitis, ataxia and abortion. In humans: antibodies reported in febrile patients and veterinary workers in Nigeria and South Africa; one historical isolation from a febrile child is cited in older literature, but a defined human syndrome is not established.
regional.headline: Simbu-serogroup virus causing neurological disease in horses and ruminants in southern Africa, with serological and occupational evidence pointing to human exposure.
regional.prevention: Vector avoidance; occupational precautions in veterinary work.
regional.geography: Sub-Saharan Africa (notably South Africa, Nigeria), with detections in Israel.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.headline: Lebombo virus. One human isolation in Nigeria.
regional.geography: Lebombo virus. One human isolation in Nigeria.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.syndrome: Fever, lymphadenopathy (a feature distinguishing it from smallpox-like illness without nodes) and a deep-seated vesiculopustular rash, often anogenital and oropharyngeal in sexually transmitted clade IIb infection. regional.prevention: MVA-BN (JYNNEOS/Imvanex) vaccination pre- and post-exposure; isolation of lesions.
regional.geography: Endemic in Central and West Africa; global clade IIb outbreak since 2022 and clade Ib expansion from eastern DRC since 2023.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.headline: O'nyong-nyong virus. Large epidemics of fever, rash and arthralgia in Africa.
regional.geography: O'nyong-nyong virus. Large epidemics of fever, rash and arthralgia in Africa.
regional.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

regional.geography: Orungo virus. Febrile illness in West Africa.

entries.syndrome: Insidious fever, sore throat, retrosternal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea; severe cases develop facial oedema, mucosal bleeding, shock and encephalopathy. Overall community case fatality ~1%, but 15–20% in hospitalised patients. Sensorineural deafness in up to a third of survivors is the hallmark sequela, and third-trimester infection carries very high fetal and maternal mortality.
entries.headline: Rodent-borne arenavirus causing 100,000–300,000 infections and thousands of deaths annually in West Africa.
entries.prevention: Rodent control, safe food storage, hospital infection control; vaccines are in clinical development (CEPI priority).
entries.geography: Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea, Benin, Ghana, Mali, Togo.
entries.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

entries.syndrome: Abrupt fever, profound weakness, myalgia, then vomiting and high-volume diarrhoea with electrolyte derangement, shock and sometimes haemorrhage. Survivors experience uveitis, arthralgia and neurological sequelae; virus persists in semen, aqueous humour and CSF, enabling late sexual transmission and relapse.
entries.headline: Filovirus causing Ebola disease, with case fatality historically 25–90%; now treatable with monoclonal antibodies and preventable by vaccination.
entries.prevention: The rVSV-ZEBOV vaccine (Ervebo) used in ring vaccination, plus the Ad26/MVA regimen; safe burial practices and infection prevention and control.
entries.geography: Central and West Africa — the 2013–2016 West African epidemic caused over 28,000 cases.
entries.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

entries.syndrome: About 80% of infections are asymptomatic; 20% develop West Nile fever; <1% develop neuroinvasive disease — meningitis, encephalitis or a poliomyelitis-like acute flaccid paralysis, with substantial mortality and long-term sequelae in older adults.
entries.headline: Globally the most widespread encephalitic flavivirus, maintained in a bird–mosquito cycle.
entries.prevention: Mosquito control and personal protection; blood-supply nucleic-acid screening; equine vaccines exist but no human vaccine.
entries.geography: Africa, Europe, Middle East, Asia, Australia (Kunjin), and across the Americas since 1999.
entries.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

entries.syndrome: Usually mild or asymptomatic: low-grade fever, maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, arthralgia. Congenital Zika syndrome — microcephaly, cerebral calcification, ocular and joint anomalies — follows infection in pregnancy. Guillain–Barré syndrome is an established post-infectious complication.
entries.headline: Flavivirus whose 2015–2016 American epidemic established it as a human teratogen.
entries.prevention: Vector control, barrier contraception or abstinence after exposure, travel advice in pregnancy. No licensed vaccine.
entries.geography: Africa, Asia, Pacific, Americas.
entries.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

entries.incubation: 1–9 days after tick bite; 5–13 days after blood contact.
entries.syndrome: Abrupt fever, myalgia, severe headache, then haemorrhagic manifestations, hepatic dysfunction and DIC. Case fatality ranges from 5% to 40%. Nosocomial outbreaks among healthcare workers are a defining feature.
entries.headline: The most geographically widespread tick-borne virus causing human haemorrhagic fever; a WHO priority pathogen requiring high-level containment.
entries.prevention: Tick protection, safe slaughter practice, and strict barrier nursing with full PPE. No licensed vaccine (a Bulgarian inactivated vaccine has limited use).
entries.geography: Africa, the Balkans, Middle East, Central and South Asia, western China; expanding with Hyalomma range into Spain and southern Europe.
entries.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

entries.incubation: Decades. Myelopathy appears after years; leukaemia typically forty to sixty years after perinatal infection.
entries.syndrome: Lifelong asymptomatic carriage in over 90%. Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL) appears after a latency of forty to sixty years, usually in those infected through breastfeeding, with a lifetime risk of a few per cent; HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP) in under 4%, presenting as spastic paraparesis with bladder dysfunction. Also infective dermatitis of childhood, uveitis, and Strongyloides hyperinfection, the last because the virus distorts the Th2 response that normally contains the worm.
entries.headline: The first human retrovirus discovered, infecting 5-10 million people. Most carry it for life without consequence; a minority develop adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma after decades, or a progressive myelopathy.
entries.prevention: Avoiding breastfeeding by carrier mothers where safe alternatives exist, which is what cut transmission in Nagasaki; leucodepletion and donor screening of blood; condoms; not sharing injecting equipment. No vaccine.
entries.geography: Sharply defined endemic foci rather than a global distribution: south-western Japan, the Caribbean, parts of South America, West and Central Africa, Iran, Romania, and Aboriginal communities of central Australia, where some adult seroprevalences exceed 40%.
entries.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

entries.incubation: Years, and progression to AIDS may not occur at all.
entries.syndrome: The same spectrum as HIV-1 — CD4 decline, opportunistic infection, AIDS — but with a longer asymptomatic phase and a substantial minority who never progress. Plasma viral loads are lower at any given CD4 count.
entries.headline: A West African lentivirus from sooty mangabeys, less transmissible and slower to progress than HIV-1, and intrinsically resistant to two whole antiretroviral classes.
entries.prevention: As for HIV-1: pre- and post-exposure prophylaxis, condoms, harm reduction, and prevention of vertical transmission. Tenofovir-based PrEP is active.
entries.geography: West Africa, with the highest prevalences in Guinea-Bissau and Senegal, and cases in Portugal, France and India reflecting historic ties.
entries.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

entries.syndrome: Usually mild or asymptomatic: low-grade fever, maculopapular rash, conjunctivitis, arthralgia. Congenital Zika syndrome — microcephaly, cerebral calcification, ocular and joint anomalies — follows infection in pregnancy. Guillain–Barré syndrome is an established post-infectious complication.

entries.prevention: Vector control, barrier contraception or abstinence after exposure, travel advice in pregnancy. No licensed vaccine.
entries.geography: Africa, Asia, Pacific, Americas.

entries.syndrome: Fever, lymphadenopathy (a feature distinguishing it from smallpox-like illness without nodes) and a deep-seated vesiculopustular rash, often anogenital and oropharyngeal in sexually transmitted clade IIb infection. Proctitis, severe pain and bacterial superinfection are common; severe disease occurs in advanced HIV.
entries.headline: Orthopoxvirus causing mpox; clade I is more virulent, clade II drove the 2022 global outbreak through sexual networks.
entries.prevention: MVA-BN (JYNNEOS/Imvanex) vaccination pre- and post-exposure; isolation of lesions.
entries.geography: Endemic in Central and West Africa; global clade IIb outbreak since 2022 and clade Ib expansion from eastern DRC since 2023.
entries.evidence_note: Human infection has been confirmed in this country.

entries.headline: Chandipura virus. Outbreaks of acute encephalitis with high mortality in Indian children.
entries.geography: Chandipura virus. Outbreaks of acute encephalitis with high mortality in Indian children.
entries.evidence_note: Virus, viral RNA or specific antibody found in the reservoir host or in livestock, with no human case reported. The virus is present in the country; whether it has ever infected a person there is unknown.
